clue.text: Perhaps kiss and run? It's easy when green

indicators.note: 'perhaps' offers one possible version of a word, so the letters come out in another possible order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to lope is to run with long easy strides

explanation.surface: A cheeky kiss-and-run, judged easy for someone young and inexperienced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' looks like it means naive, but it is the colour code: on European pistes a green run is the gentlest grade.
explanation.definitionFit: Piste grading by colour marks green runs as the beginner level, so this descriptive phrase identifies the place by its easiest category.

clue.text: Good northern paintings put up in seaside location, not going far

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up lifts it so it reads from the bottom upwards
these letters go inside the following word, which wraps around them

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
N abbreviates northern
paintings collectively are art
the shore is where land meets sea

explanation.surface: Fine northern pictures hung at a nearby resort, for someone who does not like to travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' looks like hanging the paintings on a wall; in a down clue it turns the three pieces bottom to top before they go in.
explanation.definitionFit: Weapons, flights or forecasts described this way cover only a small distance, so the hyphenated adjective means limited in reach.

clue.text: Breaks resulted in disruption

indicators.note: something in disruption has been thrown out of its proper order, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Interruptions to some activity ended up causing chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' does double duty in the surface, but it belongs to the fodder, leaving 'disruption' as the signal; the second 'in' sits inside the indicator phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Intervals between acts of a play or periods of activity are pauses, the plural noun matching the plural noun in the clue.

clue.text: Rights of foreigners first for the chop

indicators.note: chopping off the opening letter removes the front of the word

blocks.note: aliens are people from another country

explanation.surface: The entitlements of immigrants are the first to be cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the A from ALIENS. The surface invites reading the whole as a political grievance about foreigners losing rights.
explanation.definitionFit: A lien is a legal claim allowing a creditor to hold property until a debt is paid, so liens are specific legal entitlements.

clue.text: They set the course for a king and queen to appear in Olympics broadcast

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter seed widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order
turning up inside something means sitting within its letters

blocks.note: taken as written
K is king in chess notation
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen
taken letter for letter, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Royals watching the Olympic Games on television while course-setters plan the events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' suggests television coverage, but it signals scattering. 'Set the course' sounds like laying out a racetrack; it means deciding direction.
explanation.definitionFit: People who decide official policy determine the direction an organisation or government will follow, so they chart its course.

clue.text: See 15
Finally put horseradish sauce in noodle soup? That's not working

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the last letter of each word it governs
a soup is a jumbled mixture, so these letters are stirred into another order
one set of letters goes inside another, which wraps around it

blocks.note: the final letters of the three words
taken letter for letter, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cook ruining a noodle soup by stirring in horseradish sauce at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' covers all three words, not just the first. The dole is the British name for unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone receiving state unemployment payments is by definition without a job, so the idiom means unemployed.

clue.text: 25 not pale, somehow

indicators.note: 'not' tells you to take away the letters that follow
the letters removed are scattered through the word rather than sitting together, so they come out wherever they happen to fall

blocks.note: the answer to 25-across
the four letters to be removed

explanation.surface: A reference to another clue, coloured as if something is not quite pale.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike P, A, L and E from CALLIOPE wherever they fall and C, L, I, O remain in order. The preamble's 'a muse' (15) means Muses are given no definition; Clio is the Muse of history.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says Muses are left undefined; this answer is one of the nine Greek goddesses of the arts, the patron of history.

clue.text: Gummy garden gallery

blocks.note: the Garden of Eden in Genesis
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: Three adjectives that might describe a sticky outdoor art exhibit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gummy' looks like sticky but means having gums and no teeth. The Tate is a group of major British art galleries.
explanation.definitionFit: Edentate means lacking teeth, used of animals such as sloths and anteaters, so a toothless mouth is all gums.

clue.text: Aim of swat when rushing

blocks.note: first meaning: a swat is aimed at the insect itself
second meaning: doing something hurriedly, without stopping

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is literal: a swat should land on the insect. The second is the idiom for improvising in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes acting quickly while already in motion, without preparation, which is what doing things in haste involves.

clue.text: Decoration for high priest  …

indicators.note: someone high is intoxicated and muddled, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An ornament awarded to a senior cleric, with the dots leading on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High priest' reads as a single title, but 'high' is the signal. The trailing dots hand the same six letters to 12-across.
explanation.definitionFit: A stripe is a band of cloth on a uniform sleeve showing rank or service, the kind of military insignia worn as an honour.

clue.text: Sounds like "quack", for example, is inappropriate terminology

indicators.note: this phrase says the answer is pronounced like what follows rather than spelt like it

blocks.note: a quack is how a duck, a domestic bird, talks

explanation.surface: A remark that calling someone a quack is an unsuitable insult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quack' looks like the insult for a fake doctor, but here it is duck talk, the speech of poultry.
explanation.definitionFit: Swearing and obscenities are words unfit for polite company, so the idiom for cursing means improper vocabulary.

clue.text: …  and another task

indicators.note: asking for another version of the same letters means a fresh arrangement of them

blocks.note: the dots carry over the six letters of the previous clue's fodder
a chore is a routine task

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the cleric gets one more job.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots link back to 10-across: PRIEST is rearranged a second time. Terpsichore is the Muse of dance, left undefined as the preamble says.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves Muses undefined; this one is the Greek goddess presiding over dance and choral song.

clue.text: Fed up with romantic casting aspersions

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending a word up makes it read bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
amatory means relating to love

explanation.surface: Someone sick of a sentimental partner starts making disparaging remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fed up' reads as one phrase meaning bored, but the two words split into the letters and the direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Casting aspersions means making damaging insinuations about someone, which is what libellous or slanderous statements do.

clue.text: Refusal to enter Europe and make crazy all-encompassing resolution

indicators.note: something that enters goes inside, so these letters sit within the next ones
to encompass is to surround, so this word goes around everything else

blocks.note: to dement is to drive mad
EU, the European Union
no is a refusal

explanation.surface: A political tale: a veto of joining Europe, and a mad overall decision.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: the refusal goes into Europe, and that pair sits inside the verb after its first letter. 'Resolution' looks political but is the literary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The final unravelling of a plot, where its threads are tied up, is the outcome of a story's conflict.

clue.text: Recall what copper gong some heard, announcing first appetiser

indicators.note: how some people hear something is how it sounds, not how it is spelt
announcing means saying out loud, so the answer is pronounced like the wordplay

blocks.note: the phrase is rendered by sound, with the French ending heard by some as an English word

explanation.surface: Remembering the clang of a metal gong summoning diners to the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: The French phrase is often said by English speakers in an anglicised way, which the clue exploits. Its first half also names the puzzle's theme, the Muses.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny complimentary bite served before a meal, literally 'mouth-amuser' in French, is the dish that opens a restaurant dinner.

clue.text: Spirit found in this place? Most unlikely

indicators.note: an unlikely arrangement is an improbable one, so the letters are put into an odd order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter
taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A sceptic doubting a ghost could be found in this particular house.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the surface into two sentences, but 'place' and 'Most' join as fodder across it.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiritualists claimed mediums exuded a ghostly substance through which the dead materialise, so a spirit would be manifested in it.

clue.text: Brit and national leader separately entering 24

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter
each goes into a different gap rather than together, so two insertions are made

blocks.note: a melee is a fracas, the answer to 24-across
pom is Australian slang for a British person
its first letter

explanation.surface: A Briton and a foreign head of state each getting caught up in a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 is FRACAS, which must be swapped for its synonym MELEE before the letters go in. Melpomene is the Muse of tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves Muses undefined; this is the Greek goddess who presides over tragedy, often shown with a tragic mask.

clue.text: Retreating, a country's expression of gratitude to unit for work as one flying the North Atlantic

indicators.note: retreating means moving backwards, so the whole string reads the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
the UK, with the possessive S
ta is British informal thanks
the erg is a unit of work in physics

explanation.surface: A nation thanking a team for work as a transatlantic pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: The full string A, UKS, TA, ERG is read backwards in one go. 'Flying' suggests aviation, but this flier is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: This large brown predatory seabird breeds in Scotland and Iceland and ranges over northern ocean waters, so it is a North Atlantic flier.

clue.text: Time after time love comes last

indicators.note: arriving at the end means being placed after everything else

blocks.note: an era is a period of time
T abbreviates time
love is zero in tennis, and zero looks like O

explanation.surface: A romantic lament that, time and again, love arrives too late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time after time' reads as an idiom for repeatedly, but splits into two time words. Erato, fittingly, is the Muse of love poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves Muses undefined; this one presides over lyric and erotic poetry, so love is her subject.

clue.text: Before smile, spread out and wander

indicators.note: being on the outside means wrapping round what goes in

blocks.note: ere is an old word for before
a grin is a broad smile
pâté is a savoury spread

explanation.surface: Someone grinning, then stretching and setting off on a ramble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread out' looks like one verb meaning disperse, but 'spread' is the food and 'out' places it outside.
explanation.definitionFit: To peregrinate is to travel about from place to place, especially on foot, which is a formal word for roaming.

clue.text: For starters, I do love endlessly relaxing

indicators.note: starters come at the beginning, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A lazy person confessing a fondness for doing nothing, starting with the starters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' seems to call for cutting a word short, but it simply supplies its own first letter. The whole clue is also what such a person would say.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazy person who avoids work and enjoys lounging about would happily describe themselves with this statement of fondness for leisure.

clue.text: Telescopes of universities partially looking up for them

indicators.note: only part of the words is used, so the letters lie within them
in a down clue, looking up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters run across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: University observatories scanning the sky in search of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The end of 'Telescopes', 'of' and the start of 'universities' are read upwards. 'Them' points back to what the surface's telescopes are searching for.
explanation.definitionFit: Unidentified flying objects are what amateur sky-watchers hope to spot, so the pronoun stands for the things being sought overhead.

clue.text: See 8
Stole after breaking in, a recurrent disturbance

indicators.note: something recurrent runs back again, so the word is read backwards
something breaking in forces its way inside another word

blocks.note: a stole is a scarf worn round the shoulders
taken as written

explanation.surface: A burglar keeps stealing things after breaking into a house, causing repeated trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' looks like the past tense of steal, but it is the shawl.
explanation.definitionFit: A fracas is a noisy quarrel or brawl, the kind of public commotion that disturbs the peace.

clue.text: Manage to include everything by compiler

indicators.note: including something means holding it within, so the other letters go inside

blocks.note: to cope is to manage
all means everything
the setter, the compiler of the puzzle, refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: A setter's struggle to fit everything into one puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often call themselves 'compiler', standing for I. Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry, chief of the nine.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble leaves Muses undefined; this one is the Greek goddess of epic verse, said to be the eldest of the sisters.

clue.text: Blue pen written about West, if heading that way

indicators.note: travelling westwards in an across answer means going right to left, so the letters run backwards
written around something, so one word surrounds the other

blocks.note: Mae West, the American actress famed for risqué one-liners
a sty is a pen for pigs

explanation.surface: A writer using a blue pen to compose something about the American West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue pen' looks like an inkpen, but 'Blue' is the definition. Mae West is apt: her innuendo-laden films fit the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue in British usage means sexually explicit or risqué, and steamy describes erotic scenes in the same way.

clue.text: Grey pen rewritten Pinter's fourth play

indicators.note: rewriting produces a revised version, so these letters are put down in a new order
the fourth names one letter by its position in the word

blocks.note: taken letter for letter
the fourth letter of the name

explanation.surface: A dull pen redrafting a Harold Pinter drama.
explanation.walkthrough: Pinter is a red herring as a playwright; only his fourth letter is used. Peer Gynt is Ibsen's verse drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibsen wrote this Norwegian verse drama in 1867 about a roguish wanderer; it is a stage work for the theatre.
